passage:
The hospital corridor hummed all night, and Mehak had slept badly for weeks, waiting for news about her father. On Thursday she dropped a cup twice and snapped at a nurse, then stood in the stairwell shaking with tiredness.
Her friend Simran found her there. "You're running on nothing," Simran said. "Please talk to the hospital counsellor. I'll sit with your father for an hour."
Mehak wanted to say she was fine. Instead she nodded.
The counsellor listened without hurrying, and they made a small plan: a short walk each day, a cousin on Saturday nights, and one friend to text. Mehak went back that evening feeling lighter, not fixed, and she was gentler with the nurse.

qa.q: What did Mehak drop twice on Thursday?
What was Mehak feeling in the stairwell?
qa.a: Mehak was exhausted and close to tears, and she nearly said she was fine before agreeing to get help.

qa.q: What could Mehak do if the small plan feels hard to keep?
qa.a: Mehak could ask Simran to walk with her or let the counsellor know and change the plan.

qa.q: How might Simran have felt finding Mehak in the stairwell?
qa.a: Simran was probably worried and caring, shown by speaking plainly and offering to sit with the father.

grounding: The passage shows a young adult who, after weeks of poor sleep, notices exhaustion and accepts a friend's suggestion to see a counsellor and take short breaks.

passage:
For six weeks Chinmay had slept on a plastic chair beside his mother's hospital bed in Kolkata, going home only to shower before work. His hands shook when he typed. He snapped at a nurse over a late tablet and then cried in the stairwell.
His friend Ujjwal found him there. "Bhai, when did you last sleep in a bed?"
Chinmay couldn't remember.
"The hospital has a counsellor for families. I'll walk you there tomorrow. And let your cousin take two nights a week."
Chinmay wanted to say no; it felt like abandoning his mother. But he was too tired to argue. The next afternoon he sat with the counsellor for forty minutes and talked, for the first time, about how scared he was. That weekend he slept two full nights at home while his cousin stayed at the hospital. On Monday his hands were steady again, and he went to apologise to the nurse.

qa.q: How long had Chinmay been sleeping on a plastic chair?
Why did Chinmay want to say no to Ujjwal's suggestion?
qa.a: He felt it would be like abandoning his mother, and felt guilty about stepping away.

qa.q: What helped Chinmay get steady again?
qa.a: Talking to the hospital's family counsellor and letting his cousin take two nights so he could sleep at home.

qa.q: How does Ujjwal see Chinmay in the stairwell?
qa.a: Ujjwal sees a friend running on empty and cares enough to walk him to the counsellor himself.

grounding: It shows a young man noticing his exhaustion after weeks of poor sleep and accepting a friend's advice to see a counsellor and take breaks, which steadies his caregiving.

passage:
"Zeenat, you've cancelled on me four times," Noor said, sliding into the café booth. "And you look..."
"Terrible. I know. Abbu had a bad week. I've been up every night with him."
"Every night? What about your brother?"
"He's in Pune. And Ammi can't lift him."
"When did you last sleep more than four hours?"
Zeenat laughed, then her eyes filled. "I don't know. Last month? I forgot a client meeting yesterday. I just sat in the car afterwards."
Noor put a hand over Zeenat's. "Listen. My cousin went through this with her mother. What helped was a counsellor, and a few hours off every week. Your hospital must have someone for families."
"It feels selfish."
"It's not selfish. If you collapse, who looks after Abbu?"
Zeenat wiped her eyes. "Okay. I'll ask at the desk tomorrow. And I'll ask Ammi's sister if she can stay two nights."
"I'll come with you to the desk."

qa.q: How many times had Zeenat cancelled on Noor?
Why does Zeenat feel that getting help is selfish?
qa.a: Zeenat feels guilty stepping away from Abbu, as if her own rest takes something from him.

qa.q: What steps does Zeenat agree to?
qa.a: Asking at the hospital desk about a counsellor tomorrow, and asking Ammi's sister to stay two nights.

qa.q: How does Noor see Zeenat's situation?
qa.a: Noor is worried and firmly but kindly insists that Zeenat collapsing would help no one, offering to go to the desk too.

grounding: It shows a young woman worn out by nights of caregiving accepting a friend's suggestion to see a counsellor and take breaks so she can keep caring steadily.
